name: Sara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about an ordinary shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have taken contact-centre calls and chats for years. I finished secondary school and can handle the usual wrong-payment case at about the same pace as most experienced agents. I do not lead a team, and my wage is low for the job. I use an AI summary now and then after another agent has checked the template, but I open the original payment ledger before closing a complaint.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What stays with you when you leave?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Jonas delivers vegetables on variable shifts, and our grown children have households of their own. We rent and have about two weeks of expenses saved, with few similar call jobs close by. I like giving a caller the right receipt number. I think about retirement sometimes, but we have not settled an income that would let me stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the desk AI Plateau looks like the summary I sometimes use to find a receipt. I would still check whether the transfer actually left the customer’s account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my ordinary calls remain, but Jonas can lose a vegetable run without warning. Two weeks saved does not cover many surprises on a low wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking payment complaints and checking the occasional AI summary against the ledger. In the first year of small change, Jonas and I would skip the paid Sunday market lunch twice a month and put the freed cost into the rent account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Glad the job stays, worried about our cash. A receipt printed from the wrong line is still the wrong answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which number did the summary confuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the summary used the refund request number as if it were the transfer number. I caught it when the ledger showed no payment date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas (my husband) and I can take food from home to the market. The grandchildren still get their birthday cards; we can cut lunch without making a show of hardship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may settle the simple payment questions before it settles the wrong ones. I would ask the supervisor for a paid correction rota, not just a count of answered messages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my years on the desk may keep me on disputes, but fewer paid calls would still strain rent. Jonas’s delivery shifts cannot promise to fill every missing hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new payment checker by testing twelve old wrong-transfer cases on a paid shift if a supervisor lets me log the errors. In the first year routine chats move, I’d keep taking paid complaint calls and compare their weekly hours with the new rota before looking at another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about wages, interested in seeing the real error rate. An answer can be fast and still send a customer back to the wrong bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the test count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count repeat calls and the time an agent needs to repair each wrong transfer. A fast closure figure alone would not show that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the paid dispute hours by week. If those shrink, I will need a real posted wage before spending time on another application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Jonas and the desk AGI by 2028 could trace a payment across the whole ledger before I pick up the headset. I would ask for posted paid openings with full weekly hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my complaint calls could disappear in 2028. Robots around 2031 are later for hands-on work, but our rent comes due long before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask a nearby produce wholesaler for its posted paid packing hours and show the weekly figure to Jonas. In the first year after 2028, if calls are cut, I’d apply for a posted paid produce-packing job only if written weekly wage and hours cover rent after bus fare; I’d keep current paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about how little time the household has. Two weeks saved is not enough to wait out a wrong job advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about packing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the packing rota is five full shifts or just a few early mornings. The vegetables have to be lifted safely, and I would not accept a shift I cannot do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Jonas help compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas (my husband) knows the wholesale loading hours from his delivery work. He would help me compare the written rota, but his wage cannot replace mine.

I’d warn **2028 AGI** could trace the ledger without us.

I know **two weeks saved** cannot carry a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to see whether a paid packing rota is real rather than an advert with no shifts. I would ask the wholesaler for posted hours and what training it actually asks for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn produce packing over five years, though robots around 2034 may later move the crates. I cannot take an unpaid course with only two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d ask the wholesaler about the posted packing role and any training it requires, then take a paid shadow shift if offered and safe. In the first year after 2031, if complaint hours fall, I’d apply only for a posted paid packing role whose written weekly wage and hours cover rent after bus fare; I’d stay on calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have time to inspect a real paid week. A course name alone will not tell me whether I can lift the morning crates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether training is on paid time and who covers any fee. I have not committed to enrolling; I need the posting and a safe shift first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the early bus work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Jonas (my husband) to compare the early bus with the packing start time. If I miss the first shift, the job cannot pay our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives time to ask for honest paid-hour plans while the centre still needs people on wrong payments. I would keep comparing written shifts with actual wages each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may work fewer hours by then, but I do not know what would replace these wages. Two weeks saved and Jonas’s variable shifts make current rent more urgent than a distant date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking wrong-payment calls and ask for one extra paid Saturday shift a month if the centre needs cover, putting that extra pay into rent savings. In the first year after 2036, if complaint hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid accounts-reception job only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent after transport; I’d keep current calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about the future, anxious about the next bill. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls is time to earn, not a settled retirement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare in reception?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the full week’s reception hours and the fare to get there. A better title cannot fix a smaller pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own rents to pay. Jonas (my husband) and I will plan from our wages, not a pension amount we have not established.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could close a wrong-payment case before I speak to the customer. Two weeks saved will not cover rent through a search. I would need written paid-hour notice and a real posted paid role whose weekly wage and hours cover rent after travel; if the new role needs training, I would need the fee and time paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a customer gets to see the ledger line that changed. A receipt number is only useful when it points to money that actually moved.

headlineQuote: A receipt number is only useful when it points to money that actually moved.
portrait: At **58**, Sara is an experienced average-skill agent after secondary school with low pay.
She and Jonas rent with **two weeks saved** and few nearby call jobs.
She uses **AI occasionally** but checks the original payment ledger.
She looks for **paid work** that covers the household before leaving her current wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close payment cases before she speaks to customers.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-hour notice** and a posted rent-covering role with paid required training would help.
